task: Choose and fit internal wiring for a switchboard so it survives heat, overload and short circuits.
condition: Given the room temperature, the temperature allowance inside the panel, load current and the maker's cable and protection data, with design and any work done only by qualified people following local rules.
standard: The learner sizes wiring for the hotter inside temperature, names the two protection needs, and says how short runs are held against fault forces.

modules.title: Size for the hottest place
modules.intro: Air inside a closed panel is warmer than the room, and wiring often sits in the warmest zone. Cable ratings must be reduced for heat.
points: Planning rules often assume values such as about 35 °C for the panel air and as much as 55 °C where wiring runs (example values; use the current local wiring rules and the maker's data).
Choose cable size for the hotter figure, not the room.
If the room is warmer than the rule assumes, lower the allowed heat loss to stay inside the limit.
modules.example: A cable is rated 30 A at 30 °C. At 55 °C a teaching factor of 0.8 applies, so the usable rating is 30 × 0.8 = 24 A. The load is 26 A. Since 26 is more than 24, the cable fails. Step up to a cable rated 40 A at 30 °C: 40 × 0.8 = 32 A, which is above 26, so it passes with a margin of 6 A. The 30 A rating, the 26 A load and the factor 0.8 are teaching figures, and real factors come from the maker's tables.
modules.activity: A load is 18 A. Cable options are rated 20 A, 25 A and 32 A at 30 °C. Use a factor of 0.8 and say which is the smallest that passes.
modules.standard: Learner derates the rating for heat and picks the smallest passing cable.

modules.title: Pick the right cable
modules.intro: Not every cable suits a hot, tight space. Insulation type and how cables are bundled both matter.
points: Use heat-resistant insulation rated for high conductor temperatures.
Halogen-free types give less smoke if there is a fire.
Thin conductors are usually laid in ducts and bundles, heavier ones in air in small bundles.
modules.example: A panel has 12 control wires, each carrying 1 A, packed in one duct. A second run has 2 heavy cables carrying 60 A each. In the duct, heat from 12 wires builds up, so each wire loses some rating, which is acceptable because 1 A is small against the wire's rating. The two heavy cables are laid apart in air, each with room around it, so each loses less rating. Putting the 2 heavy cables into the crowded duct as well would raise the heat and risk the insulation. Total of 14 conductors in the duct would be unwise for this mix. All figures are worked-example values.
modules.activity: List four wires in a panel, two thin control wires and two heavy power cables. Decide where each goes (duct, air, bundle) and why.
modules.standard: Learner matches thin wires to ducts and heavy cables to open air, and names insulation needs.

modules.title: Two different problems
modules.intro: Overload and short circuit are different faults needing different checks. Wiring must survive both until protection acts.
points: Overload is a slow rise in current, so protection must match the cable's current rating.
Short circuit is a sudden, very large current, so the cable must survive until the device clears it.
Where a device limits fault current, the section between busbar and device may sometimes be sized for the smaller load, but only a qualified designer can decide this from the maker's data.
modules.example: A cable has a derated rating of 24 A and a protective device rated 20 A. Because 20 is below 24, the device protects the cable from overload. A device rated 32 A would not, since 32 is above 24. For a short circuit, the maker's table says this cable can carry a fault for 0.1 s at the available fault level. The device clears in 0.01 s, which is 10 times faster than the limit, so the cable passes. If the device took 0.5 s instead, it would fail. Figures are examples only.
modules.activity: Choose which device protects a cable that derates to 36 A against overload, from devices of 32 A and 40 A. Then say what extra check short circuit needs.
modules.standard: Learner picks the device that protects against overload and states the clearing time check.

modules.title: Hold short wiring firmly
modules.intro: In a short circuit, conductors push apart with great force. Short runs are especially at risk because they sit close and carry the full fault.
points: Keep short runs tight and supported at the spacing the maker gives.
Use cable supports or run them in plastic ducts.
Never leave loose loops or unsupported lengths near busbars.
modules.example: A run of 0.6 m between a busbar and a device has one support at the middle only. The maker asks for a support every 150 mm. At 0.6 m, that means 600 ÷ 150 = 4 sections, so about 3 supports along the run plus the ends. With only one support, each half of 300 mm is twice the allowed gap of 150 mm. The run is under-supported and fails the check. Add supports until no gap exceeds the maker's figure. Spacing here is an example.
modules.activity: Calculate how many gaps and supports a 450 mm run needs with a support every 150 mm, and compare with a layout that has one support in the middle.
modules.standard: Learner calculates the supports needed and judges whether a layout is acceptable.

quiz.q: Which temperature should inside-panel wiring be sized for?
quiz.a: The hotter temperature where the wiring runs, not the room temperature.

quiz.q: A cable is rated 30 A at 30 °C and the factor is 0.8. What is the usable rating?
The load is 26 A and the usable rating is 24 A. Pass or fail?
quiz.a: Fail, so step up to a larger cable.
It gives less smoke if there is a fire.

quiz.q: Where are heavy conductors usually laid?
quiz.a: In air, in small bundles, not packed in crowded ducts.

quiz.q: Why should 2 heavy cables not join 12 wires in a crowded duct?
quiz.a: Heat builds up and risks the insulation.

quiz.q: A cable derates to 24 A. Does a 20 A device protect it from overload?
A device clears in 0.01 s and the cable limit is 0.1 s. Does it pass?
quiz.a: Yes, it clears 10 times faster than the limit.

quiz.q: A 600 mm run needs supports every 150 mm. How many gaps are there?
quiz.a: Four gaps of 150 mm, so about three supports between the ends.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: A hot box
ladder.slide: Cutaway of a closed panel with a thermometer reading much higher than the room.
ladder.notes: Start by asking where it is hottest in a panel. Introduce that wiring sits in the warm zone.

ladder.title: L2 Explain: Derating
ladder.slide: A sum 30 × 0.8 = 24 A beside a cable and a thermometer.
ladder.notes: Explain why rating drops with heat. Say the 0.8 factor is for teaching and the maker tables are the source.

ladder.title: L3 Apply: Pick a size
ladder.slide: Load 26 A, three cables rated 25, 30 and 40 A at 30 °C.
ladder.notes: Learners derate each and pick the smallest that passes. Answer is the 40 A cable at 32 A usable.

ladder.title: L4 Analyse: Two faults
ladder.slide: Two columns: overload slow rise, short circuit sudden surge, with clearing time arrows.
ladder.notes: Draw out the difference. Use the 20 A device and 24 A cable, then the 0.01 s against 0.1 s check.

ladder.title: L5 Design: Lay it out
ladder.slide: Panel sketch with a duct, an open-air zone, a busbar and a short run to a device.
ladder.notes: Learners assign each wire to a place and mark supports. Remind them all design and fitting belongs to qualified people following local rules.

ladder.title: L6 Evaluate: Find the faults
ladder.slide: A layout with an undersized cable, a crowded duct and one support on a 0.6 m run.
ladder.notes: Learners list the faults and rank them. Compare their lists in pairs.

ladder.title: L7 Create: Wiring plan
ladder.slide: Blank plan: loads, temperature, cable size, protection, supports, review.
ladder.notes: Each learner makes a plan for an invented small panel. Collect and discuss one. Close with the safety message again.

rubric.meets: Derates for the hotter inside figure and picks a passing cable.
rubric.exceeds: Checks the result against the maker table and a margin.

rubric.not_yet: Packs all wires together without thought.
rubric.meets: Matches insulation, ducts and open air to the wire type.
rubric.exceeds: Explains the heat effect of bundling with numbers.

rubric.not_yet: Treats the two faults as the same.
rubric.meets: Checks device rating against cable rating and clearing time against the limit.
rubric.exceeds: Also explains when a limiting device lets a section be sized smaller.

rubric.not_yet: Leaves short runs loose or suggests untrained work.
rubric.meets: Supports short runs at the maker spacing and says qualified people do the work.
rubric.exceeds: Calculates supports and inspects a layout critically.

jobs.what: Cuts, routes and fits internal wiring to the approved design.
Reviews wiring sizes and protection against the design rules before build.
Inspects and tests finished panels and records the results.
Checks cable supports, routing and labelling against the build standard.
